examples.problem_statement: |x^3| < 64. Quantity A: -x. Quantity B: -|x|. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Apply the absolute value identity to |x^3| < 64, splitting it into the two cases the book uses: the inside taken as positive, and the inside taken as negative.
Take the cube root of the positive case to get the upper bound on x.
Multiply the negative case by -1, flipping the inequality sign as the book notes, then take the cube root to get the lower bound on x.

solution.result: x \text{ may be positive, negative, or zero}
solution.description: Combine the two bounds into a single interval, and observe that this interval does not fix the sign of x.

solution.operation: \text{compare } -x \text{ and } -|x| \text{ for } x \ge 0 \text{ and for } x < 0
solution.result: \text{equal when } x \ge 0; \ \text{Quantity A greater when } x < 0
solution.description: Test both sign cases in the two quantities: with x positive or zero the quantities match, with x negative Quantity A is larger, so no single relationship holds.

key_reminders: |a| = a when a is positive or zero, and |a| = -a when a is negative
Multiplying an inequality by -1 flips the inequality sign
A quantitative comparison is (D) whenever two allowed values of the variable give different relationships
common_mistakes: Dropping the negative case and concluding only x < 4, which would hide the negative values that make Quantity A greater
Forgetting to flip the sign when multiplying x^3 > -64 through by -1
Assuming -x is always negative, which makes the two quantities look permanently equal

concept.technique_name: unit digit pairing for divisibility by 10

examples.problem_statement: If n is a natural number, then what is the sum of all the possible distinct remainders when 9^n + 6^n + 4^n + 11^n is divided by 10?

solution.result: 0 \ \text{when } n \text{ odd}; \ 2 \ \text{when } n \text{ even (last digit of } 9^2 + 11^2)
solution.description: Pair the first and last terms and check their combined last digit: the pair is divisible by 10 for odd n, and leaves 2 for even n.

solution.result: 0 \ \text{when } n \text{ odd}; \ 2 \ \text{when } n \text{ even (last digit of } 6^2 + 4^2)
solution.description: Pair the middle two terms the same way: divisible by 10 for odd n, leaving 2 for even n.
Add the two pair remainders for odd n, giving no remainder when 10 divides the whole expression.
Add the two pair remainders for even n to get the remainder in that case.
Sum the distinct remainders found across the two cases to answer what the question asks for.

key_reminders: A remainder on division by 10 is just the last digit of the expression
Terms can be grouped in pairs whose last digits cancel to 0
Powers of 9, 11, 6 and 4 behave differently for odd and even exponents, so both parities must be checked
common_mistakes: Reporting 4 as the only remainder and ignoring the odd-n case that contributes remainder 0
Summing the remainders 2 and 2 as the final answer without first separating the odd and even cases
Pairing the terms as 9^n + 6^n and 4^n + 11^n, whose last digits do not combine to a multiple of 10

concept.sub_category: Data Sufficiency on income, expenditure and savings ratios

examples.problem_statement: Directions: The following question is accompanied by three statements A, B and C. You have to determine which statement(s) is/are sufficient/necessary to answer the question. Income of P is 1 2/3 of the income of Q. The expenses of P, Q and R are in the ratio of 6 : 4 : 5. Find the expenses of Q. A. Expenses of R is Rs 2000 less than that of P. B. P's saving is Rs 3000. C. Income of R is one-third of the total incomes of P, Q and R of Rs 36000. 1) Only B and C together are sufficient 2) Only A alone is sufficient 3) All together are necessary 4) Either B and C together or A alone is sufficient 5) All even together are not sufficient

solution.description: Use statement A: the gap between P's and R's expense ratio shares is one unit, and that gap is stated to be Rs 2000, which fixes the value of a single ratio unit.
Multiply Q's four ratio units by the unit value found, giving Q's expense from statement A alone, so A alone is sufficient.
Use statement C: R's income is one-third of the Rs 36000 total, so divide the total by 3.
Subtract R's income from the total to isolate the combined income of P and Q.
Substitute the given income relation between P and Q into the combined income to solve for P's income.
Use statement B: subtract P's saving from P's income to get P's expense.
Convert P's expense into one ratio unit and scale it to Q's four units, so B and C together also give Q's expense; either route works, giving option 4.

key_reminders: A difference between two ratio shares can be equated to a stated rupee difference to fix one ratio unit
In data sufficiency, once one route answers the question, keep testing the other statements before choosing a combination option
common_mistakes: Reading 'income of P is 1 2/3 of Q' as P = 1.23Q or as a 1 : 3 relation instead of P = 5/3 Q
Stopping after statement A works and choosing option 2, missing that B and C together also suffice
Applying the Rs 2000 difference to Q's share instead of to the single unit gap between P and R

concept.technique_name: equivalent rule substitution in an ordering game

examples.problem_statement: Detectives investigating a citywide increase in burglaries questioned exactly seven suspects - S, T, V, W, X, Y, and Z - each on a different one of seven consecutive days. Each suspect was questioned exactly once. Any suspect who confessed did so while being questioned. The investigation conformed to the following: T was questioned on day three. The suspect questioned on day four did not confess. S was questioned after W was questioned. Both X and V were questioned after Z was questioned. No suspects confessed after W was questioned. Exactly two suspects confessed after T was questioned. Which of the following, if substituted for the rule that exactly two suspects confessed after T was questioned, would have the same effect both in determining the order in which suspects were questioned and in identifying which suspects confessed during questioning? (A) The final suspect to confess was the sixth suspect questioned. (B) W and the suspect questioned immediately before W were the last two suspects to confess. (C) W was the last suspect to confess. (D) The suspects questioned fifth and sixth both confessed. (E) S was questioned last and immediately after W.

solution.operation: T \ \text{in slot } 3, \ \text{exactly two C's after T}
solution.description: Unpack the original rule: since T sits third, the two confessions after T and the two non-confessions must all fall in slots four through seven.
Apply the separate rule that the fourth suspect did not confess, removing one N from the block and leaving the rest for slots five to seven.
Order the remaining letters using the rule that nobody confesses after W, which forces the N to the end and places W and S in the last two slots.
Check answer (A) against the chain: it puts a C in slot six but leaves slot five unfixed, so it does not reproduce the full effect.

solution.operation: \text{test (B): } W \ \text{and the suspect before } W \ \text{are the last two C's}
solution.result: W \ \text{could sit in slot } 2 \ \text{with N's in } 3\text{-}7
solution.description: Check answer (B): it looks like it forces W into slot six, but it also permits W in slot two with every later suspect not confessing, an arrangement the original diagram forbids.

solution.result: W \ \text{could sit in slot } 1 \ \text{or } 2; \ \text{slot } 5 \ \text{not forced to } C
solution.description: Check answer (C): it has the same defect as (B) plus the defect of (A), since it neither pins W late nor forces a confession in slot five.
Check answer (D): a confession in slot six plus the no-confession-after-W rule pushes W and S into slots six and seven, rebuilding exactly the same consequences as the original rule.
Check answer (E): it fixes an order but says nothing about who confessed, so it fails to reproduce the confession pattern and (D) stands.

key_reminders: An equivalent rule must reproduce every downstream inference of the original, not just one of them
The chain here runs: two C's after T, then two C's and one N in slots 5-7, then C C N with W and S in 6 and 7
Because no one confesses after W, any confession late in the order pins W's position
common_mistakes: Choosing (B) because W confessing alongside the prior suspect feels like it forces W into slot six, when W in slot two also satisfies it
Accepting (A) on the strength of slot six alone without checking that slot five must also be a confession
Treating (E) as equivalent because it fixes W and S at the end, overlooking that it never establishes any confession
